Onion prices double as India’s food inflation climbs to 7.74 per cent
Data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation (MoSPI) on October 12 show that onion inflation reached 108.09% in September, up sharply from 48.78% in August. 
India’s year-on-year food inflation rose to 7.74% in September 2026, from 5.97% in August, with onion prices more than doubling over the previous 12 months. The food-price surge pushed headline retail inflation to 5.54%, the highest reading under the new CPI series with the base year 2024 = 100 since October 2024.
Data released by the Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation (MoSPI) on October 12 show that onion inflation reached 108.09% in September, up sharply from 48.78% in August. Ginger prices rose 62.85% year-on-year, garlic 54.62% and lemon 36.41. These increases were not uniform across the food basket. Potato prices fell 11.50% from a year earlier, while tomato prices declined 8.62%.
The pressure was greater in rural India. Food inflation stood at 8.06% in rural areas in September, compared with 7.18% in urban areas. Rural headline inflation reached 6.08%, against 4.88% in cities. The rural-urban gap matters because food typically accounts for a larger share of expenditure among lower-income households.
International markets are also recording higher prices. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization’s Food Price Index averaged 136.0 points in September, up 1.5% from August and 5.8% from a year earlier.
The FAO’s cereal price index rose 5.1% month on month and was 17.2% higher year-on-year. Its vegetable-oil index increased 0.9% during September and was 18.3% higher year-on-year, while the sugar index rose 6.1% month on month and 14.7% year-on-year.
Onions, in particular, are sensitive to domestic harvests and seasonal supply. Establishing the extent of international price transmission would require a commodity-level comparison of import prices, wholesale prices and retail prices over several months.
The FAO itself cautions that sustained global price pressures may pass through to consumers, especially in import-dependent countries, but that is a risk assessment rather than evidence of causation for India’s September vegetable spike.
The immediate test is whether fresh crop arrivals ease domestic supply constraints. The FAO has warned that strengthening El Niño conditions could add uncertainty to production, particularly for rice in South and Southeast Asia. It forecasts global cereal production in 2026 to fall 2.1% from 2025, although the projected harvest would remain the second-largest on record.
For India, the next CPI release—scheduled for November 12, 2026—will show whether the September surge remained concentrated in a few vegetables or spread more widely across the food basket. Until then, the relative roles of domestic harvests and global market pressures in shaping household food bills remain uncertain.

Applications are open for the Atlantic Fellows for Social and Economic Equity (AFSEE) Programme 2027-2028. Policymakers, researchers, activists, practitioners, artists, and movement-builders from around the world are invited to apply to the innovative, fully-funded, and inequalities-focused fellowship programme based at the International Inequalities Institute at the London School of Economics and Political Science.
Currently recruiting for its eleventh cohort, the AFSEE Fellowship is aimed at mid-career social-change leaders who have at least seven years of experience in challenging inequalities. Applications are accepted from individuals working on any field of social and economic equity, including, but not limited to economic and social rights; sustainability and environmental justice; tax justice and economic alternatives; women’s, minority, and disability rights; rights to education; public policy; housing and urban inequalities; labour rights; community organising; arts and culture; and peacebuilding and transitional justice.
Launched in 2016, the AFSEE Programme celebrates its tenth anniversary in 2026-2027; working towards its aim to build a 400-strong inspiring community of Fellows over two decades. In its first ten cohorts, the programme has brought together over 160 change-makers from 60 countries across the globe.

opportunities-727d963a77.headline: FUSE Society Blueprint 2026
opportunities-727d963a77.fulltext:
Blueprint is a one-week digital hackathon for secondary school students, organized by FUSE Society in partnership with Free Geek.
Participants will identify a business challenge facing a real company and design a digital solution to address it, demonstrating analytical rigour, creativity, and commercial judgment. Each team will submit a solution together with a recorded presentation explaining the work. The winning team will receive a grand prize of $250.
No prior programming experience is required. Under the core evaluation criteria, submissions are assessed on the quality of the analysis and the suitability of the proposed solution rather than on technical polish, and a clickable prototype produced in a design tool is scored on equal terms with a coded application.
A separate Technical Execution bonus of up to [10] points is available at both judging stages to teams submitting a functioning technical build. The bonus is additional to the core criteria, is capped at [10] points of a possible [100], and is never used to resolve a tie between teams.
A complete submission consists of three components. All three must be finished by the Day 7 deadline. A Devpost project page alone does not constitute a submission.
Each team must publish a project page to the Blueprint hackathon page. The page must state the problem identified, the proposed solution, an implementation outline addressing cost and timeline, and the names of all team members. The solution artifact must be attached to or linked from this page, whether as an uploaded file, an embedded design link, or a repository link. The project page must be published rather than saved as a draft.
Each team must record a presentation of no more than 8 minutes explaining the solution and the reasoning behind it. Where practical, each team member should appear or speak.
The recording must be uploaded to YouTube with the visibility set to Unlisted. Recordings set to Private cannot be accessed by the judging panel and will not be scored. Teams are advised to test the link in a private browsing window before submitting.
The submission form is the step that formally enters a team into the competition. The form requires the team name; the names, ages, schools, and countries of all members; a team contact email address; the Devpost project link; the YouTube presentation link; an artificial intelligence usage disclosure; and confirmation that the team has read and accepts these rules.
A confirmation email will be sent within 24 hours of submission. Teams that do not receive confirmation should contact the Organizers immediately rather than assume the submission was received.
Teams may resubmit the form at any point before the deadline; the most recent entry will be treated as final.

climate-energy-cad85b53aa.headline: China Proposes Export Controls on 12 Solar Technologies; India’s Clean-Energy Manufacturing Faces New Questions
climate-energy-cad85b53aa.fulltext:
China's proposed export controls could affect access to selected solar-manufacturing technologies and influence international supply-chain decisions.
China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used in solar-equipment manufacturing, citing national security concerns. The proposal covers technologies associated with advanced solar cells, thin silicon wafers and polysilicon production. Some technologies could face export prohibitions, while others would be subject to restrictions rather than a complete ban. For India, which is seeking to expand domestic solar manufacturing and reduce dependence on overseas technology, the proposal raises questions about equipment access, technology transfers and the future competitiveness of its renewable-energy supply chain. The measures are proposed, and their final scope will depend on the regulatory process.
Context, analysis and verified insights that explain the story beyond the headline.
China has developed a major position in global photovoltaic manufacturing through large-scale industrial capacity, specialised suppliers, extensive production networks and sustained investment in solar technology. India, meanwhile, has been expanding its domestic solar manufacturing base to support renewable-energy deployment and strengthen supply-chain resilience. Solar manufacturing is technologically complex. A production facility may depend on specialised equipment for wafer processing, cell formation, coating, material treatment and quality control. Access to advanced production techniques can influence both the cost and performance of the finished product. Export controls can affect this ecosystem by limiting the transfer of particular manufacturing processes or requiring additional government approvals. Their impact varies according to the scope of the rules and the availability of alternative technologies.
China has proposed new export controls covering 12 technologies used to manufacture solar equipment, a move that could affect the international renewable-energy industry and countries seeking to build their own photovoltaic manufacturing capabilities.
The proposal was reported by Reuters on 18 October 2026, following a regulatory announcement by China's Ministry of Commerce. The measures form part of a wider revision of China's technology export-control catalogue, which also covers areas such as artificial intelligence and biotechnology.
Location: China, with potential implications for international solar supply chains, including India.
Action Taken: A proposed revision to the technology export-control catalogue was announced, with public consultation scheduled to close on 15 November 2026.
Impact: Manufacturers may face additional restrictions or licensing requirements for selected technologies. The final consequences for Indian industry remain uncertain.
Chinese authorities have cited national security concerns as the reason for increasing oversight of photovoltaic technologies. The ministry has argued that these technologies are increasingly relevant to sensitive sectors, including aerospace and national defence.
The proposal is significant because China occupies a central position in the global solar manufacturing industry. Its companies and industrial ecosystem play major roles in producing solar equipment, manufacturing components and developing processes used across the photovoltaic supply chain.
However, the proposal should not be interpreted as an immediate, blanket ban on all Chinese solar technology exports. The reported measures distinguish between technologies that could be prohibited from export and advanced manufacturing technologies that would face restrictions.
Solar manufacturing is increasingly connected to national energy security, industrial policy and international technology competition. For India, access to advanced production technology can influence how quickly domestic manufacturers expand capacity, improve efficiency and reduce reliance on external suppliers. The proposal could encourage greater investment in local research and equipment development. It could also create near-term challenges for companies whose production plans depend on technology covered by the final controls. For the global renewable-energy industry, the key issue is whether the proposed rules change the availability of specialised manufacturing processes and how companies adapt their supply chains. The practical impact will depend on the final regulatory framework, not simply on the announcement of proposed controls.
The proposed controls include technologies associated with the production of thin silicon wafers, perovskite solar cells, tandem solar cells and large-scale fluidised-bed polysilicon manufacturing.
Thin silicon wafers are important components in photovoltaic cells. Manufacturing methods that reduce wafer thickness can influence material consumption, production efficiency and the cost structure of solar equipment.
Perovskite solar cells represent an emerging class of photovoltaic technology that has attracted research interest because of their potential for high conversion efficiency and flexible manufacturing approaches. Their commercial prospects depend on continued improvements in stability, durability, production scale and performance.
Tandem solar cells combine different light-absorbing materials, such as perovskite and silicon, to capture a wider portion of the solar spectrum. The approach has the potential to improve energy conversion efficiency, although commercial performance and manufacturing costs remain important considerations.
The proposal also covers technologies used in large-scale fluidised-bed production of polysilicon, a key raw material for solar panels. This production method can offer advantages in energy consumption and cost compared with the conventional Siemens process, depending on the specific manufacturing configuration.
The precise effect of the proposed controls will depend on the final list of covered technologies, licensing requirements and the circumstances of individual exports.
The reported proposal also identifies advanced solar-cell manufacturing technologies, including TOPCon, heterojunction technology (HJT) and XBC, for restrictions rather than a complete export prohibition.
TOPCon, or tunnel oxide passivated contact technology, is used to improve the efficiency of silicon solar cells. HJT combines crystalline silicon with thin layers of other semiconductor materials to improve cell performance. XBC refers to back-contact cell designs that place electrical contacts on the rear side of a solar cell to reduce front-side shading.
These manufacturing methods matter because solar producers compete on conversion efficiency, manufacturing costs, equipment reliability and the ability to scale production.
If the proposed controls make particular technology transfers more difficult, manufacturers outside China may need additional licensing, alternative equipment suppliers or greater investment in domestic research and engineering.
That does not mean production outside China would necessarily stop. The actual consequences would depend on the technology involved, the availability of substitutes and whether individual transactions receive the necessary approvals.
India has been working to expand its domestic solar manufacturing capacity as part of its broader renewable-energy and energy-security objectives.
Building a domestic manufacturing ecosystem involves more than assembling finished solar panels. Producers also need access to specialised machinery, production processes, engineering expertise, industrial materials and reliable component supply chains.
China's proposed controls could therefore become relevant to Indian manufacturers if their expansion plans depend on technology transfers or equipment affected by the final regulations.
The potential consequences include longer procurement timelines, additional compliance requirements, changes in supplier selection and greater pressure to develop alternative production methods.
The scale of any impact remains uncertain. Not every solar manufacturer relies on the same equipment, and the proposal does not automatically prohibit all imports of Chinese solar products or every form of technology collaboration.
India's response will depend on how the final Chinese rules are written, which technologies are covered and whether Indian companies have access to viable alternatives.
Tighter controls on technology transfers could strengthen the incentive for India to invest in domestic research, equipment manufacturing and advanced photovoltaic production.
Indian companies could benefit over the longer term if they develop competitive manufacturing processes, establish alternative technology partnerships or improve their ability to produce specialised equipment domestically.
However, these outcomes are not guaranteed. Developing sophisticated solar manufacturing technologies requires investment, engineering expertise, research facilities, skilled workers and reliable commercial-scale production.
A change in Chinese export policy would not automatically make Indian manufacturers more competitive. The benefits would depend on how quickly domestic firms could address technological gaps and whether their products could compete on efficiency, quality and cost.
For policymakers, the development reinforces the importance of treating technology access as a component of industrial strategy rather than focusing exclusively on the number of solar panels manufactured.
The proposed solar restrictions are part of a broader review of Chinese technology export controls, which also includes artificial intelligence and biotechnology.
Advanced technologies increasingly have both commercial and strategic applications. Governments are paying greater attention to how specialised equipment, production knowledge and technical expertise move across borders.
For manufacturers, this creates an additional layer of regulatory risk. A company may need to consider not only the price and performance of equipment but also export licences, technology-transfer rules and the possibility of future restrictions.
Such controls can influence investment decisions because manufacturing facilities are designed around particular processes, equipment suppliers and technical specifications. Replacing a specialised production system may require significant time and capital.
The broader policy shift also highlights the relationship between trade regulation and industrial competitiveness. Countries seeking technological independence must consider how to maintain access to global expertise while building their own research and manufacturing capabilities.
The measures remain subject to the regulatory process. According to Reuters, the public consultation on the proposed changes is scheduled to close on 15 November 2026.
Exporters have also been required to register certain overseas technology transfers while the export-control catalogue is being updated.
The final impact will depend on the completed catalogue, the scope of any restrictions, applicable licensing procedures and how authorities implement the measures.
Until those details are established, it would be premature to describe the proposal as a comprehensive ban on China's solar exports or to predict a specific increase in Indian solar-panel prices.
The next important milestone is the completion of China's public consultation and the publication of the final regulatory provisions. Manufacturers and technology suppliers will need to assess which processes fall within the final catalogue, whether licences are required and how existing contracts or planned technology transfers will be treated. Indian industry stakeholders will also need to determine whether their manufacturing plans depend on any of the affected technologies and whether alternative suppliers or domestic development programmes can meet their requirements. ai-5b7c72137e.headline: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?
ai-5b7c72137e.fulltext:
Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about.
Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each.
In addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort.
“It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.”
The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet.
That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the Russian NotPetya and North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide.
Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. The Anthropic team predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.”
Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House.
“The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.”
Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows a paper published by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm.
“The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan.
Guan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said.
“Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne. “It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own.”
Anthropic did not respond to an interview request.
Outside Washington, many in the AI and security worlds believe greater government oversight of AI is now essential. But members of Congress have introduced mutually conflicting bills, while the White House has so far created only a small review board.
Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants.
“The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.”

deep-tech-d778aafa40.headline: Ukraine launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia as spat between Trump and Zelenskyy continues
deep-tech-d778aafa40.fulltext:
[Text below is CNBC's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Ukraine launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia as spat between Trump and Zelenskyy continues
Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war.
The strikes came as tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepened, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and the prospect of further U.S. sanctions against Moscow still uncertain.
Trump said Sunday that he decided to hold off on implementing new sanctions on Russia because he doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."
In a social media post, the U.S. president defended his Friday order to issue a waiver to prevent new sanctions from being placed on Moscow from bipartisan criticism that he was favoring Russian President Vladimir Putin's interests over those of Ukraine. Trump said he believed new sanctions would undermine negotiations to bring about a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.
"I can sign it later, or any time that I want!" Trump added about the sanctions.
Trump also lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has been critical of Trump's recent outreach to Putin, for launching strikes on Russian energy infrastructure during the conflict, claiming Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war."
Zelenskyy: Waiving sanctions strengthens Russia
Speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press" earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin's war effort. He also said U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being "blocked for some period of time."
Zelenskyy said that while he trusted Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a "historic mistake" for Washington.
"People want to forget what's going on. But we can't give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth," Zelenskyy said. "We can't compare me and Putin. He's (an) aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He's a terrorist. And that's why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position."
Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as "next steps in diplomacy."
Two killed as Russia and Ukraine trade blows
One person was killed and five others were wounded in the St. Petersburg attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city's Ruchi oil depot, local Gov. Alexander Beglov said. The companies confirmed that a logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion but could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed, and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.
Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says
Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4½-year-old war, but offered no details. Kyiv reported Russian attacks on energy sites continued after Trump's announcement, and on Thursday said it had resumed strikes on Russian oil facilities after a three-day pause.
Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday that Russia had attacked Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since Trump's announcement. The Ukrainian government initially said it was observing the ceasefire.
He said energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, and accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote.
Ukraine apology to Lithuania over drone alert
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry apologized on Sunday after a drone entered Lithuania's airspace, prompting authorities to issue an air raid warning.
Russian electronic warfare may have diverted the drone during a Ukrainian operation against legitimate military targets in Russia, ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement.
Lithuanian authorities urged residents in two northern counties along the Latvian border to take cover early Sunday because of a possible drone incursion, public broadcaster LRT reported.
A drone entered the northern Pasvalys region and damaged a moving car, LRT said, citing Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center. No injuries were reported.

global-economics-d3b9f69d24.headline: AI Trade Reversal Pierces Asia’s Star Picks-and-Shovels Stocks
global-economics-d3b9f69d24.fulltext:
BloombergPublished18 Oct 2026, 06:14 AM IST
(Bloomberg) -- A deepening selloff in US technology stocks is exposing a new vulnerability in Asia’s artificial intelligence trade: mounting financing costs could choke off the spending needed to sustain the boom, threatening earnings across a supply chain that has powered the region’s stock-market rally.
The pressure intensified last week as oil surged to $110 a barrel for the first time since May, stoking inflation concerns, and investors turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. An eight-session rout in US semiconductor shares — the longest since 2008 — wiped roughly 16% off the sector’s benchmark, while the Nasdaq 100 suffered its worst week since April 2025.
For Asia, where chipmakers and the hardware suppliers that make printed-circuit boards, precision components and manufacturing equipment have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI frenzy, the implications could be significant heading into Monday’s open.
A Goldman Sachs Group Inc. basket of regional AI hardware stocks tumbled 11% last week, its steepest decline since mid-July. The selloff showed little sign of abating despite an upbeat revenue outlook from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., underscoring how concerns over AI spending are spreading across the hardware supply chain.
Some of Asia’s standout performers were hit particularly hard in the maelstrom. Nan Ya Plastics Corp., a maker of printed circuit board materials and the best-performing stock on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index this year, tumbled 12% from a record high. Rival Unimicron Technology Corp., the index’s second-best performer, fell 14% in a week, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co., which makes an array of electronic components, plunged 23%.
“Financing costs are like gravity for the AI boom,” said Jian Shi Cortesi, a fund manager at GAM Investment Management in Zurich. “Rising borrowing costs could make infrastructure projects harder to finance and delay spending. Even a delay could trigger a reset in Asian suppliers’ earnings expectations and valuations.”
The concern is no longer just whether demand for AI chips will hold up. It’s whether hyperscalers and neocloud operators can keep financing the infrastructure needed to deploy them — and whether the expected returns will justify the scale of investment.
Bonds of neocloud provider CoreWeave Inc. sank to levels signaling distress last week as investors questioned whether AI demand and revenue could support the borrowing behind its expansion. Its shares slumped 12% on Friday, resulting in the stock’s worst week since November with a 25% drop. The episode brought the financing risks of the boom into sharper focus, with surging oil prices adding to worries that inflation could keep borrowing costs elevated.
While TSMC, SK Hynix Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co. supply the chips and memory needed for AI computing, their earnings ultimately depend on continued investment in the infrastructure that uses those products. Component makers and equipment suppliers face the same underlying risk, potentially with less visibility into the timing of individual projects.
“AI funding stress is a bigger challenge for downstream beneficiaries than for the core compute ecosystem,” said Kevin Net, portfolio manager at Financiere de l’Echiquier in Paris. “Basically, the further away you get from the actual chip, the greater the risk you might see timing delays.”
Warnings about funding risks have come from industry executives, including Broadcom Inc. Chief Executive Officer Hock Tan, who said capital, rather than shortages of memory chips or manufacturing capacity, would become the biggest constraint on AI growth.
Gartner Inc. has warned that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as investment threatens to outpace the revenue needed to justify it.
“If hyperscalers and neoclouds cannot fund their datacenter investments, that would translate into lower orders for Asia enablers like TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix,” said Vey-Sern Ling, managing director at Union Bancaire Privee. “Given how jittery the market is, the read-through would be very negative for the semi picks and shovels.”
The stakes are particularly high for Asian equities, where the AI buildout has become a dominant investment theme. TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix together account for nearly a third of the MSCI Asia ex-Japan Index and about a fifth of the index provider’s broader Asian gauge, with their suppliers adding to the region’s exposure to the same spending cycle, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
Eight of the 10 best-performing companies in the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index this year are component makers, each having gained at least 236%. Those gains leave earnings expectations and valuations vulnerable if spending growth slows or projects are pushed back.
Still, there is little evidence so far that financing strains have translated into weaker orders, and some investors remain confident that robust demand will sustain the sector.
“We are not worried about the ongoing chip selloff,” as demand for AI remains strong, said Kunjal Gala, head of global emerging markets at Federated Hermes Ltd. in London. Gala’s fund is overweight on Korea and owns TSMC shares.

Known as the JIOUSDT contract,the crypto-based futures contract would let traders speculate on Jio Platforms’ pre-IPO price movements. They can participate in it without actually owning its shares.
What is JIOUSDT?
JIOUSDT is a pre-IPO perpetual futures contract. It lets traders use a speculative financial instrument tied to the company’s anticipated market valuation. As per Bitget website, it can be traded 24x7, year-round and are settled directly in USDT. Jio pre-IPO perpetual futures will offer up to 20x leverage, with funding fees settled every eight hours.
How does it work?
The contract has traded around the clock since its launch on Wednesday, October 14, with its price hovering near $ 11.9. Perpetual futures contracts have no expiry, with periodic funding payments between longs and shorts that help keep prices aligned with the underlying market.
Traders can participate in JIOUSDT by making positions on market expectations for Jio valuation. The financial instrument would let traders capture speculation around event-driven moves related to Jio IPO, subscription demand, and grey market premium (GMP).

EU condemns Israeli settler attack on diplomats in occupied West Bank
EU demands accountability after settlers attack European diplomats amid violence against Palestinian olive farmers.
The European Union has condemned an attack by Israeli settlers on a convoy carrying European diplomats in the occupied West Bank and called for action to stop the pogroms.
The 27-member bloc issued its statement on Sunday, the day after masked settlers attacked a visiting delegation near the Palestinian village of Taybeh.
The assault has intensified diplomatic pressure on Israel as attacks on Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest increasingly threaten journalists and foreign visitors accompanying them.
Diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland, along with representatives of the Catholic Church, were visiting the predominantly Christian village east of Ramallah to show support for Palestinian olive growers when masked men attacked them.
They threatened members of the delegation and smashed a window of a Belgian diplomatic vehicle.
Bernard Baudoux, the 78-year-old mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, said he was kicked and beaten, despite wearing the ceremonial sash identifying him as a French official.
“I was thrown to the ground,” Baudoux told the Reuters news agency on Saturday.
The EU said on Sunday it welcomed statements by Israeli officials condemning the attacks but expected “full accountability” and measures to prevent further violence against Palestinians and journalists.
It also called on Israel to respect international law and stop expanding settlements in the occupied territory.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called on Israel on Saturday to arrest those responsible and protect civilians.
Prevot said Belgian personnel were safe, although their vehicle had been damaged.
Poland’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement posted on X on Saturday evening that its diplomats were unharmed and there was no indication they had been specifically targeted.
Warsaw demanded an explanation from Israel and action against the attackers.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the violence on Saturday, describing the perpetrators as rioters and said that police had opened an investigation.
He also criticised the delegation for failing to coordinate its visit with the Israeli military, arguing that advance arrangements could have helped protect the visitors.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said violence against diplomats was unacceptable but questioned whether video circulating online provided enough evidence to establish exactly what happened.
Violence during olive harvest
The diplomatic incident followed another attack on Friday in the village of Abu Falah, near Ramallah. Masked settlers assaulted Palestinians harvesting olives and severely injured US photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was covering the farmers for The Washington Post.
Levine said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes, despite wearing protective clothing identifying her as a journalist.
She suffered broken ribs and underwent surgery on her hand. Her camera, phone and passport were stolen.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Maryland on Saturday, urged Israel to crack down on settler pogroms and warned that President Donald Trump did not want another crisis in the West Bank.
In a statement on X on Saturday evening, the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee described Levine’s assault as a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions.
The attacks have disrupted an olive harvest that provides income for tens of thousands of Palestinian families.
On Sunday, Israeli settlers cut down 120 olive trees on Palestinian-owned land in the village of Kisan, southeast of Bethlehem, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Farmers have reported assaults, stolen crops, damaged trees and restrictions preventing them from reaching their land.
The United Nations humanitarian office said last week that nearly 200 settler attacks linked to this year’s harvest had caused casualties or property damage, already exceeding the 185 incidents recorded throughout last year’s season.
